title: What training does the Clery Act require colleges to provide?
description: What 34 CFR 668.46 requires as at November 2026: prevention programs for new students and employees, ongoing campaigns, and annual training for officials.
shortAnswer: The Jeanne Clery Disclosure of Campus Security Policy and Campus Crime Statistics Act, as amended by the Violence Against Women Reauthorization Act of 2013, requires colleges in federal student aid programs to run primary prevention and awareness programs for all incoming students and new employees, ongoing prevention campaigns, and annual training for officials who conduct disciplinary proceedings on dating violence, domestic violence, sexual assault and stalking. The rules are at 34 CFR 668.46.
keyTakeaways: 34 CFR 668.46(j)(1)(i) requires primary prevention and awareness programs for all incoming students and new employees, with six mandatory content elements.
668.46(j)(1)(ii) requires ongoing prevention and awareness campaigns for students and employees, sustained over time.

668.46(k)(2)(ii) requires that disciplinary proceedings be conducted by officials who receive annual training on these crimes and on investigation and hearing processes that protect victim safety and promote accountability.
The programs must be described in the annual security report, which must be distributed to enrolled students and current employees by October 1 each year (34 CFR 668.41(e)).
The regulations do not expressly require training for campus security authorities, but institutions must count crimes reported to them, so CSA training is the practical control.
regulator: Federal Student Aid (FSA), US Department of Education
appliesTo: Institutions of higher education that participate in the federal student aid programs under Title IV of the Higher Education Act of 1965
All incoming students and new employees (primary prevention and awareness programs)
Officials who conduct investigations, meetings and hearings in disciplinary proceedings for dating violence, domestic violence, sexual assault and stalking
Campus security authorities, as defined in 34 CFR 668.46(a)

sections.heading: Where do Clery Act training duties come from?

blocks.text: The training duties come from section 485(f) of the Higher Education Act, codified at [20 U.S.C. 1092(f)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/20/1092), and the Department of Education's regulations at [34 CFR 668.46](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-34/section-668.46). The prevention program and annual training requirements were added by the Violence Against Women Reauthorization Act of 2013 amendments, which is why they are often called the VAWA amendments to Clery.

The statute requires institutions to describe "primary prevention and awareness programs for all incoming students and new employees" (20 U.S.C. 1092(f)(8)(B)(i)) and requires that disciplinary proceedings "be conducted by officials who receive annual training" on domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault and stalking (1092(f)(8)(B)(iv)(I)(bb)). The implementing regulation, published at 79 FR 62783 on October 20, 2014, sets the detail.

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects 34 CFR 668.46 and 668.41 as published in the eCFR as at November 2026. The Federal Register shows no amendment to section 668.46 since the October 20, 2014 final rule. Department guidance documents and handbooks can change separately from the regulation and should be checked on the Federal Student Aid site before relying on them.

sections.heading: What must primary prevention and awareness programs cover?

blocks.text: Every incoming student and new employee must receive a program covering six specific elements. Under 668.46(j)(1)(i), the institution's annual security report must describe its primary prevention and awareness programs "for all incoming students and new employees", which must include:

items: A statement that the institution prohibits dating violence, domestic violence, sexual assault and stalking, as defined in 668.46(a).
The definitions of dating violence, domestic violence, sexual assault and stalking in the applicable jurisdiction.
The definition of consent, in reference to sexual activity, in the applicable jurisdiction.
A description of safe and positive options for bystander intervention.
The information described in 668.46(b)(11) and (k)(2), which covers reporting procedures, victim rights and options, and how disciplinary proceedings work.

blocks.text: The jurisdictional definitions matter for content owners. Item 2 and item 3 require the state law definitions where the campus sits, so a multistate institution may need location specific versions rather than one national module. A program that teaches only the institution's own policy definition of consent does not meet item 3 by itself.

The regulation also defines what counts as primary prevention. Under 668.46(j)(2)(iv), primary prevention programs are programming, initiatives and strategies "informed by research or assessed for value, effectiveness, or outcome" that are intended to stop these crimes before they occur by promoting healthy behaviors, encouraging safe bystander intervention, and seeking to change behavior and social norms. An institution should be able to show the research basis or the evaluation behind its chosen program.

sections.heading: What are ongoing prevention and awareness campaigns?

blocks.text: Ongoing campaigns are the sustained, institution wide follow up to the initial program, directed at all students and employees. Section 668.46(j)(1)(ii) requires the annual security report to describe the institution's "ongoing prevention and awareness campaigns for students and employees", including the same six elements listed in (j)(1)(i)(A) to (F).

Section 668.46(j)(2)(iii) defines these campaigns as programming, initiatives and strategies "that are sustained over time" and focus on understanding and skills for addressing these crimes, "using a range of strategies with audiences throughout the institution". A single annual email does not fit that definition well. The definition of programs to prevent these crimes in 668.46(a) adds that programs should be culturally relevant, inclusive, sustainable, responsive to community needs, and consider risk and protective factors at individual, relationship, institutional, community and societal levels.

The rule sets no hours, format or frequency for either the initial program or the ongoing campaigns. Institutions set those cycles themselves; [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles) explains how to document that choice so it can be defended.

sections.heading: Which officials need annual training, and on what?

blocks.text: Every official who conducts a disciplinary proceeding for dating violence, domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking must be trained at least annually. Section 668.46(k)(2)(ii) requires that proceedings "be conducted by officials who, at a minimum, receive annual training on the issues related to dating violence, domestic violence, sexual assault, and stalking and on how to conduct an investigation and hearing process that protects the safety of victims and promotes accountability".

The trained population is wider than hearing panels. Section 668.46(k)(3)(iii) defines a proceeding as "all activities related to a non-criminal resolution of an institutional disciplinary complaint, including, but not limited to, factfinding investigations, formal or informal meetings, and hearings". Investigators, informal resolution staff and appeal officers who take part in that process are therefore within scope.

The same paragraph sets standards the training should prepare officials to meet. Under 668.46(k)(3)(i), a prompt, fair and impartial proceeding is completed within reasonably prompt timeframes set by policy, is transparent to both parties, gives timely notice of meetings and equal access to information, and is "conducted by officials who do not have a conflict of interest or bias for or against the accuser or the accused". Section 668.46(m) also prohibits retaliation against anyone exercising rights or responsibilities under the section.

Many of the same officials handle sexual harassment complaints under Title IX, which has its own training topics and a seven year record duty. See [Title IX training requirements](/regulations/title-ix-training-requirements) for how the two sets of requirements fit together.

sections.heading: Do campus security authorities have to be trained?

blocks.text: The regulation does not expressly require training for campus security authorities (CSAs), but an institution cannot report its crime statistics accurately without it. The statute requires statistics of offenses "reported to campus security authorities or local police agencies" (20 U.S.C. 1092(f)(1)(F)), so a CSA who does not recognize or pass on a report creates an undercount.

Section 668.46(a) defines four categories of CSA: a campus police or security department; individuals with campus security responsibility, such as those who monitor entrance to institutional property; any individual or organization named in the institution's security policy as someone to whom crimes should be reported; and an official with "significant responsibility for student and campus activities", including student housing, student discipline and campus judicial proceedings. Pastoral and professional counselors acting in that role are excluded.

Because the fourth category is defined by function, coaches, residence life staff and student activity advisors can be CSAs without a security job title. A role based approach, described in [role based training](/glossary/role-based-training), is the usual way to identify and train them.

sections.heading: How is compliance reported, and what are the penalties?

blocks.text: Compliance is disclosed through the annual security report, and violations can lead to civil penalties. Under [34 CFR 668.41(e)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-34/section-668.41), an institution must distribute its annual security report to all enrolled students and current employees "by October 1 of each year", and 668.46(b)(11) requires the report to describe the prevention programs and campaigns required by paragraph (j).

Under 20 U.S.C. 1092(f)(14), where the Secretary determines that an institution has substantially misrepresented the number, location or nature of crimes required to be reported, the Secretary imposes a civil penalty in the same amount and by the same procedures as under section 1094(c)(3)(B). The inflation adjusted maximum for a 1094(c)(3)(B) penalty is listed in [34 CFR 36.2](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-34/section-36.2) as $71,545 as at November 2026.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry starts from the six content elements in 668.46(j)(1)(i) and the two annual training topics in (k)(2)(ii), mapping each to a learning outcome and an assessment point before content is written. Jurisdiction specific definitions are held as separate, versioned components, so a change in one state's law updates only the affected programs.

faqs.q: Does the Clery Act require annual training for all employees?
faqs.a: No. The annual training requirement in 668.46(k)(2)(ii) applies to officials who conduct disciplinary proceedings. New employees must receive a primary prevention and awareness program, and all employees must be reached by ongoing campaigns, but the regulation sets no annual frequency for general staff training.

faqs.q: Do online courses satisfy the primary prevention requirement?
faqs.a: The regulation does not prescribe a format. It requires the six content elements and that primary prevention programs be informed by research or assessed for value, effectiveness or outcome. An online course can meet the requirement if it covers every element, including the definitions that apply in the campus jurisdiction, and the institution can show its basis or evaluation.

faqs.q: When did the VAWA training requirements take effect?
faqs.a: The Violence Against Women Reauthorization Act of 2013 amended the Clery Act, and the Department of Education's implementing regulation was published in the Federal Register on October 20, 2014 at 79 FR 62783. Section 668.46 has not been amended since, according to the eCFR as at November 2026.

faqs.q: Are graduate students and transfer students incoming students?
faqs.a: The regulation says all incoming students and does not exclude any category, so institutions generally treat new graduate, transfer and online students as incoming. Institutions should state their interpretation in policy and apply it consistently, because the annual security report must describe the programs offered to all of them.
